Homeland Security Secretary Michael Chertoff said opposition from people such as Tamez will not derail the fence.

“Can we simply abandon an enterprise because it is a problem for a particular individual?” Chertoff told CNN. “I don’t think I can accept that.”

Chertoff argues that building the fence would reduce the ongoing flow of undocumented immigrants crossing the border, help limit drug trafficking, and improve safety for Border Patrol agents who have encountered rising levels of violence.

The government’s goal is to build 700 miles of fencing along the U.S.-Mexico border, with 370 miles planned for completion by the end of this year. If federal officials proceed as planned, about 70 miles of fence will be built in the Rio Grande Valley before year’s end.

Along this section of the border, the Rio Grande itself serves as a natural divider, though in certain spots the river is narrow enough for people to swim across. Evidence of such crossings is visible along the riverbanks. Piles of underwear are left behind by people who swim over, then change into dry clothing they carried in plastic bags before vanishing into the United States.

In the Rio Grande Valley, the Border Patrol has increased its presence and surveillance efforts, adding more lighting and motion-detecting sensors. A levee running beside the river has a muddy road on top, which Border Patrol vehicles use to monitor the area.

Richard Cortez, mayor of the border city of McAllen, Texas, says the border would be better secured by hiring additional Border Patrol agents, making the Rio Grande deeper, and removing tall vegetation from the riverbanks rather than building a fence.

Cortez describes the proposed barrier as “a multibillion-dollar speed bump” that may delay illegal crossings but will not prevent them.

“It is a false sense of security,” he said. “America will not be safe. America will continue to waste resources on something that is not going to work.”

Cortez and other border-town mayors opposed to the fence have organized under the name Texas Border Coalition. The group sent a letter to Chertoff requesting more consultation about the fence, but the Department of Homeland Security rejected that request this week.

David Pagan of U.S. Customs and Border Protection wrote in an e-mail that although the agency supports open communication with local residents and officials, “We do not plan to suspend work on the construction of fence in order to hold a series of additional consultation meetings.”

Cortez said McAllen is considering a legal challenge to the law requiring construction of the border fence.

That leaves a confrontation underway between the federal government and about 100 landowners, including Eloisa Tamez, who remain unwilling to yield.

“I will not allow them to come and survey my land. I have an American-given right to protect my property,” she said.

counterfactuals.output:
**Texas landowner fights border fence cutting through ancestral property**

**EL CALABOZ, Texas** — For Eloisa Tamez, the fight over the federal government’s border fence is not an abstract debate about immigration policy or national security. It is a battle over family history, sovereignty and land she says has belonged to her people for generations.

Tamez, a longtime resident of El Calaboz, a small community near Brownsville in South Texas, has resisted federal efforts to build a border barrier across her ancestral property along the Rio Grande. The land, she says, is tied to her family’s heritage and to the Indigenous Lipan Apache community, making the government’s plans deeply personal.

“This is not just property,” Tamez has said in public statements about the dispute. “This is our history.”

The federal government began pursuing segments of border fencing in the Rio Grande Valley following legislation passed after the September 11 attacks and amid growing political pressure to strengthen the US-Mexico border. Under the Secure Fence Act of 2006, hundreds of miles of fencing were authorized along parts of the southern border.

But in South Texas, the geography of the Rio Grande and the location of private land complicated construction. Unlike in some western states, much of the borderland in Texas is privately owned. That meant federal officials often needed access to farms, ranches and homesteads that had been in families for generations.

Tamez became one of the most visible landowners to challenge the government’s efforts.

Federal officials argued that the barrier was necessary for border security and sought access to survey and eventually build on portions of private land. When some landowners refused, the government turned to condemnation proceedings, using eminent domain to acquire property or access rights.

Tamez opposed those efforts, saying she was not properly consulted and that the project would divide her land, disrupt daily life and separate her from parts of her property. Critics of the fencing plan also argued that it would damage wildlife habitat, interfere with flood control and place some US land between the fence and the river — effectively leaving homes, farms and historic sites on the “south” side of the barrier while still inside the United States.

Civil liberties groups, environmental advocates and Indigenous rights organizations rallied around Tamez’s case, viewing it as emblematic of the broader tensions surrounding border enforcement in the Rio Grande Valley.

Supporters say her resistance highlighted questions about due process and the unequal burden placed on small landowners. While some large landholders and politically connected properties were able to avoid fencing or negotiate changes, critics argued that poorer communities and Indigenous families had fewer resources to fight the federal government.

For Tamez, the issue has always extended beyond compensation.

She has described the land as inherited, sacred and inseparable from her identity. Building a fence through it, she and her supporters argue, represents not only a physical barrier but a continuation of historical displacement of Indigenous people in the region.

The Department of Homeland Security has maintained in past border wall disputes that barriers are one tool among many used to secure the border, direct crossings toward monitored areas and assist Border Patrol agents. Federal officials have also said they work with landowners where possible, though legal challenges have repeatedly questioned how those negotiations are conducted.

The fight in El Calaboz became part of a larger national conversation that has continued through multiple presidential administrations. Border wall construction, halted in some places and revived in others, remains one of the most contentious issues in American immigration politics.

In the Rio Grande Valley, stretches of fencing already stand near neighborhoods, farms and wildlife refuges. In some areas, the barrier does not sit directly on the international boundary but farther inland, creating a patchwork of access roads, gates and isolated parcels.

For Tamez and other landowners, the lasting concern is what happens after the headlines fade.

The fence, they say, changes not only the landscape but the relationship between communities and the land that sustains them.

“I was born here,” Tamez has said. “My ancestors were here. And I have a right to remain here.”

Her resistance has made El Calaboz a symbol of the human cost of border infrastructure — a place where national policy meets a family’s front yard, and where one woman’s refusal to give up her land continues to echo in the broader debate over security, property rights and justice along the border.

**DHS Sues Texas Border Landowners Over Access for Border Fence Surveys**

**McALLEN, Texas —** The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has moved to take legal action against Texas landowners who have refused to allow federal surveyors onto their property as the government presses ahead with plans to build new border fencing along the U.S.-Mexico line.

The lawsuits, filed in federal court, seek temporary access to private land in the Rio Grande Valley so government crews can conduct surveys, environmental assessments and engineering work for fencing authorized by Congress. The legal action marks a sharp escalation in the dispute between Washington and South Texas property owners, local officials and activists who say the project threatens homes, farms, wildlife habitat and historic family land.

Homeland Security officials argue that the surveys are a necessary first step in securing areas of the border that they say are vulnerable to illegal crossings and smuggling. But many landowners have resisted signing access agreements, saying they have been given little information about where the fence would go, how much land would be affected, or whether they would be fairly compensated.

One of the most prominent opponents is **Eloisa Tamez**, a Lipan Apache landowner and nursing professor in Cameron County whose family has held land near the border for generations. Tamez has said the government’s approach ignores the history and rights of border families.

“I feel like my land is being taken away from me,” Tamez said, describing the federal push for access as an attempt to force property owners into accepting a project they do not support. She has argued that the fence would divide communities and cut residents off from portions of their own land near the Rio Grande.

Federal officials maintain that the government has the authority to obtain access for survey work and, if necessary, to acquire land through eminent domain. Homeland Security Secretary **Michael Chertoff** has defended the department’s aggressive timeline, saying border security must take precedence.

“If I have to make a choice between the interests of a few landowners and the interest of the country in protecting the border, I’m going to choose the country,” Chertoff said in remarks defending the fence program.

The planned fencing in Texas has proved especially contentious because, unlike in parts of Arizona and California where much border land is federally owned, large stretches of the Texas border run through private property, farms, ranches, cities and wildlife refuges. In the Rio Grande Valley, the proposed route does not always follow the river itself, meaning some landowners fear they could end up with property trapped between the fence and the international boundary.

Local officials have also criticized the federal government’s handling of the project. **McAllen Mayor Richard Cortez** said city leaders support border security but object to a one-size-fits-all barrier that could damage local communities and the region’s economy.

“We are not against border security,” Cortez said. “But we are against a wall that divides our community and does not take into account the reality of life along the border.”

Cortez and other Rio Grande Valley officials have urged the federal government to consider alternatives, including levee improvements, technology, lighting, cameras and increased Border Patrol staffing. They say local governments were not adequately consulted before plans moved forward.

The Department of Homeland Security has said the access lawsuits are limited in scope and are intended only to allow surveyors to determine where fencing might be built. However, opponents say the surveys are the first step toward condemnation proceedings and eventual seizure of land.

Civil-liberties groups, environmental organizations and property-rights advocates have joined some landowners in challenging the federal government’s plans. Environmentalists warn that fencing could disrupt migration corridors and damage sensitive habitat in the Lower Rio Grande Valley, one of the most biologically diverse regions in the country.

The legal fight comes as the federal government faces deadlines to complete hundreds of miles of fencing under border-security legislation passed by Congress. Chertoff has also been granted authority to waive certain environmental and land-use laws to speed construction, a power that has drawn criticism from lawmakers and advocacy groups.

For landowners like Tamez, the dispute is about more than survey crews or fence lines. It is a battle over heritage, sovereignty and the meaning of security in communities that have existed along the border for centuries.

“This is my home,” Tamez said. “My roots are here. The government should not be able to come in and treat people as if they do not matter.”

The lawsuits are expected to proceed in federal court as DHS seeks access orders allowing survey work to begin. If the courts side with the government, landowners who continue to resist could face further legal action as the border fence project moves forward.

## Rio Grande Valley Pushes Back Against Planned Border Fence

Opposition is growing in the Rio Grande Valley over federal plans to build additional fencing along the U.S.-Mexico border, with local residents and officials arguing that the project threatens private property rights, disrupts communities, and fails to address the realities of illegal immigration in the region.

Much of the proposed fence route would cut through privately owned land, farms, ranches, wildlife areas, and neighborhoods along the Rio Grande. Landowners have expressed frustration that the federal government could use eminent domain to gain access to their property, saying they are being asked to sacrifice land that has been in families for generations.

For many residents, the debate is not only about border security but also about property rights. Some landowners worry that fencing could separate them from portions of their own land, block access to irrigation systems, or reduce the value and usefulness of their property. Others argue that Washington is imposing a one-size-fits-all solution without understanding the geography and economy of South Texas.

Local officials in the Valley have also criticized the plan. County judges, mayors, and other community leaders have said that a border fence would damage relations with Mexico, interfere with trade and tourism, and create practical problems for border communities that depend on cross-border movement. They contend that the Rio Grande Valley’s needs are different from those of other border regions and should not be addressed solely through barriers.

Illegal immigration remains a major concern in the area, and many residents acknowledge the need for stronger border enforcement. However, opponents of the fence argue that the project would do little to stop determined migrants or smugglers, who may find ways around, over, or under the barrier. They instead call for more Border Patrol personnel, better technology, improved infrastructure at ports of entry, and immigration reforms that address labor demand and legal pathways.

Environmental concerns have also played a role in the opposition. The Rio Grande Valley is home to sensitive wildlife habitat, refuges, and flood-control systems. Critics say fencing could fragment habitat, interfere with drainage, and create flooding risks if barriers are placed near levees or riverbanks.

Supporters of the fence argue that physical barriers are an important tool for border security and can help reduce illegal crossings in high-traffic areas. But in the Rio Grande Valley, many local leaders insist that security measures must be balanced with respect for landowners, local economies, and the region’s unique relationship with Mexico.

The conflict has placed Valley communities at the center of a national debate over immigration enforcement, federal authority, and the rights of property owners. As planning continues, residents and officials are urging the federal government to consult more closely with local communities before moving forward.

**[CNN TRANSCRIPT-STYLE REPORT — ORIGINAL SCRIPT]**

**ANCHOR:**  
Tonight, a battle over border security is playing out not in Washington, but on small parcels of private land in South Texas. In the tiny community of El Calaboz, near Brownsville, families who have owned land for generations are confronting the Department of Homeland Security over plans tied to hundreds of miles of border fencing.

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
El Calaboz, Texas, is quiet farmland, a place of mesquite trees, irrigation canals, and family property lines that often go back decades. But for roughly 100 landowners in this part of the Rio Grande Valley, the federal government’s plan to build border fencing has turned their land into the center of a legal and political fight.

The Department of Homeland Security says fencing is necessary to help secure the U.S.-Mexico border. The broader plan calls for hundreds of miles of barriers — about 700 miles in all — along stretches of the southern border.

But here, residents say the project is cutting through more than land. They say it threatens homes, farms, wildlife habitat, and a way of life.

**LANDOWNER:**  
This is not just property to us. This is our family history. My parents worked this land, my grandparents worked this land. Now we’re being told the government can come in and take part of it.

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
DHS has sought access to private property to survey land and prepare for construction. Some owners have refused to sign permission forms, forcing the government to pursue court action. Federal officials argue they have the authority to move forward under laws passed by Congress to speed border barrier construction.

**DHS STATEMENT:**  
The Department of Homeland Security is committed to securing the border while working with affected property owners. Border infrastructure is one tool used to prevent illegal crossings, drug smuggling, and other threats.

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
But many residents say the process has felt rushed and one-sided. Some say they were given confusing paperwork. Others say they were warned that if they did not cooperate, the government could take them to court.

Attorneys and advocates working with landowners say many families lack the resources to fight the federal government.

**ATTORNEY FOR LANDOWNERS:**  
These are not large corporations. These are individual families, retirees, farmers. They are being asked to give up access to land, sometimes without clear answers about compensation, gates, drainage, or how the fence will affect their daily lives.

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
The geography of the Rio Grande Valley makes the issue especially complicated. In some places, the proposed fencing would not sit directly on the river. Instead, it could be built north of the Rio Grande, leaving homes, farmland, or wildlife areas between the fence and the actual border.

That has led some residents to ask whether they will effectively end up on the “wrong side” of the barrier.

**LANDOWNER:**  
If the fence goes behind my land, then what happens to us? Do we need a gate to get to our own property? Who controls that gate? What happens in an emergency?

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
Environmental groups are also raising concerns. The lower Rio Grande Valley is home to sensitive habitat and wildlife corridors used by species such as ocelots and migratory birds. Critics say walls and fencing could fragment that habitat and worsen flooding in low-lying areas.

Supporters of the fencing argue that border communities have long dealt with illegal crossings and that physical barriers help Border Patrol agents respond more effectively. They say national security must come first.

**LOCAL RESIDENT WHO SUPPORTS FENCING:**  
People here want safety, too. If fencing helps reduce crime or helps Border Patrol, then we have to consider it. The question is how to do it fairly.

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
That question — fairness — is at the heart of the dispute in El Calaboz. Landowners say they are not opposed to security, but they want transparency, compensation, and respect for property rights.

For now, the conflict is moving through courtrooms, community meetings, and kitchen-table conversations across South Texas. What looks on a map like a line of fencing is, on the ground, a line through families, farms, and the meaning of private property.

**ANCHOR:**  
And as construction plans move forward, the fight in El Calaboz underscores a larger national debate: how to balance border security with land rights, environmental concerns, and the lives of people who live along the border every day.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed news piece about a Texas woman whose family land dates back to a 1767 Spanish grant and who vows to fight government efforts to survey and build a border fence on her property.
counterfactuals.output:
**Texas Landowner Vows to Fight Border Fence on Family Property Tied to 1767 Spanish Grant**

*By Staff Writer*

CAMERON COUNTY, Texas — On a quiet stretch of land near the Rio Grande, where mesquite, brush and open pasture give way to the river that marks the U.S.-Mexico border, a Texas woman says her family’s history is rooted deeper than any modern boundary line — and she is prepared to fight the federal government to protect it.

The property, she says, has been in her family for generations, tracing its origins to a Spanish land grant issued in 1767, long before Texas became a republic, a state or a flashpoint in the national immigration debate. Now, the land has become the center of a confrontation over the federal government’s efforts to survey and construct sections of border fencing across private property in South Texas.

Federal officials say access to the land is necessary to secure the border and carry out congressional mandates for fencing and related infrastructure. The landowner, however, argues that the project threatens not only her property rights but also a centuries-old family legacy and the cultural heritage of communities that have lived along the river for generations.

“I’m not giving up my land,” she has said in public statements and interviews about the dispute. “This land is my history. It is my family’s history.”

The standoff reflects a broader conflict unfolding across parts of the Rio Grande Valley, where government plans for border barriers have collided with privately owned ranches, farmland, historic tracts, wildlife refuges and communities whose ties to the land predate the United States itself.

### A Family Claim Older Than Texas

The woman’s property is located in South Texas near the border, in an area where land titles often have complex histories tied to Spanish and Mexican grants. In the 18th century, the Spanish crown issued large tracts of land to settlers in what was then northern New Spain. Many families in the Rio Grande Valley continue to trace ownership, inheritance and identity to those original grants.

Her family’s claim, she says, dates to one such grant from 1767. Over time, the original tract was divided, inherited and passed through generations. For descendants, such land is more than real estate; it is a connection to ancestors, culture and survival.

That history is central to her opposition. She argues that federal officials are treating the land as an obstacle to be crossed rather than as a living part of a family’s identity.

“This is not empty land,” supporters of landowners in the region have often said. “These are homesteads, burial grounds, farms, ranches and sacred places.”

### Federal Survey Efforts Spark Resistance

The dispute escalated when federal authorities sought access to the property to conduct surveys related to border fence construction. Such surveys typically precede planning, engineering and potential condemnation actions. Federal officials may seek court orders allowing entry if landowners refuse permission.

The government has argued in similar cases that survey access does not immediately take ownership of the land but allows engineers and planners to assess where barriers, roads, gates, lighting or other infrastructure might be placed. Landowners counter that survey crews are often the first step toward seizure, construction and permanent alteration of their property.

In border fence cases, the federal government has relied on authority granted by Congress to build barriers along the southern border. When private property is involved, officials may pursue condemnation through eminent domain, a legal process that allows the government to take land for public use if it provides compensation.

But for landowners like this Texas woman, the issue cannot be reduced to a payment.

“How do you compensate someone for generations?” one local advocate asked. “How do you put a price on land that has been in a family since before the United States existed?”

### Property Rights and Border Security

The case sits at the intersection of two powerful political and legal forces: border security and private property rights.

Supporters of border fencing say barriers are a necessary tool to deter illegal crossings, drug trafficking and human smuggling. They argue that the federal government has both the authority and the responsibility to secure the international boundary. In their view, disputes over individual parcels should not prevent broader security efforts approved by Congress.

Opponents say walls and fences in the Rio Grande Valley are uniquely disruptive. Unlike some areas where the border runs through desert or federal land, much of the South Texas border is privately owned. Because the Rio Grande itself twists and bends, fencing is often built north of the river, sometimes cutting through farms and leaving homes, fields or river access on the “south” side of the barrier — even though they remain within the United States.

Landowners fear being trapped between the fence and the river, losing access to irrigation, livestock areas or family sites. Environmental groups have also warned that barriers can fragment habitat, worsen flooding and disrupt wildlife migration corridors.

### A Community With Deep Roots

The woman’s resistance has drawn attention from property-rights advocates, Indigenous rights groups, civil liberties organizations and local residents who see her case as emblematic of the Rio Grande Valley’s complex history.

Many families in the region identify as Mexican American, Tejano or Indigenous, and their presence along the river predates the modern border. For them, the border did not define the community so much as divide it. Families, churches, cemeteries and trade routes historically stretched across both sides of the Rio Grande.

The planned fence, critics say, deepens that division.

“It is not just a wall between countries,” one supporter said. “It can become a wall through people’s lives.”

The woman has emphasized that her opposition is not simply political but personal. She sees herself as a steward of land inherited from ancestors and intended for future generations. Allowing a fence to cut through it, she argues, would break faith with both.

### Legal Battle Looms

If the federal government presses forward, the dispute could move through federal court. In previous border fence cases, courts have often granted the government access to survey land and, in many instances, allowed condemnation proceedings to continue. However, landowners may challenge the scope of access, demand procedural protections or contest compensation.

Civil liberties attorneys have criticized the speed and scale of some border land actions, arguing that landowners may not fully understand their rights or may feel pressured to sign agreements. They have urged residents to seek legal counsel before granting access or accepting compensation.

For the Texas woman at the center of this dispute, the legal fight is also a moral one. She has vowed to resist survey crews and challenge any attempt to take or alter the property.

“I have rights,” she has said. “My family has rights. And this land has a history that deserves respect.”

### Part of a Larger Border Fight

The controversy comes amid decades of debate over border barriers, from the Secure Fence Act of 2006 to later expansions under multiple presidential administrations. While the politics of border security often play out in Washington, the consequences are felt most directly in places like Cameron County, Hidalgo County and Starr County, where individual landowners can find themselves facing the federal government.

In the Rio Grande Valley, even small tracts can carry immense historical weight. A few acres may represent a family’s last physical connection to an original grant, a vanished village or a way of life tied to the river.

As federal officials continue to pursue border infrastructure, the woman’s pledge to fight has become a reminder that the land along the border is not merely a line on a map. It is home, inheritance and memory.

For now, she says, she is staying put.

“They may have power,” she has told supporters, “but we have our history. And I will not let them erase it.”
